questiontext.text:
The diagram shows two triangles:

  • \(\triangle ABC\) (blue) is the original.
  • \(\triangle A_1B_1C_1\) (red) is its image after a single transformation.

generalfeedback.text:
Answer: {@description@}.

A reflection flips the shape over a mirror line, so the image is "back to front": each vertex ends up the same perpendicular distance from the line, on the opposite side.

Explore: drag the blue vertices to make your own triangle, choose a mirror line, and compare with your group. Use Clear to start again.

truefeedback.text: You have correctly spotted that this is a reflection — but that is not the right mirror line. The mirror line lies halfway between each point and its image, at right angles to the line joining them. Look at where just one vertex, say \(A\), maps to.

Look at the orientation. Under a rotation the triangle would keep its sense (going \(A\rightarrow B\rightarrow C\) the same way round). Here \(\triangle A_1B_1C_1\) is a mirror image — flipped over — so it is a reflection, not a rotation.
A translation slides every point the same distance in the same direction, keeping the shape facing the same way. Here the image has been flipped over, so it is a reflection, not a translation.
It is a transformation: every point of \(\triangle ABC\) has a matching image point in \(\triangle A_1B_1C_1\), the same shape and size. Decide whether it has been slid, turned, or flipped.
